pron_note: Also heard as TYE-rayd, stress on the first syllable — both are standard.
means:
A **long, angry, abusive speech** — a sustained verbal attack, usually delivered at volume and at length.

The word passes judgement on the speaker, not the target. Calling something a tirade says the person lost control, went on far too long, and stopped persuading anyone several minutes ago. Nobody describes their own outburst as a tirade; it is what other people call it afterwards. Length is essential — a single cutting remark can never be one.
trick_line: **Tirade** begins with **tire** — it rants on until everyone in the room is tired of it.
trick_unpack: The hidden word carries the key nuance: a tirade is defined by exhausting length, not just anger.
sentences: His resignation letter degenerated into a three-page **tirade** against colleagues who had, by then, stopped reading.
She launched into a **tirade** about the parking situation and we just stood there holding our coffees.
in_the_wild: Newsroom boilerplate: "launched into a foul-mouthed **tirade**" is the standard phrase for a footballer at a referee or a politician caught on a hot mic — you've read the sentence a hundred times.
etymology: French **tirade**, from Italian **tirata** = *"a pull, a long drawn-out stretch,"* from **tirare**, "to pull." A tirade is speech *drawn out* — the same *tirer* gives English **retire** (to draw back).
root: tirare / tirer (to pull, to draw out)
